articles.body_html:
I've been quietly building Antigravity Tools — a collection of 59 free, browser-based developer utilities — and today I'm sharing everything I built and learned.

Why vanilla JS? No React, no build step.

The main constraint I set for myself: zero dependencies, zero server, zero telemetry.

When you paste your JWT token into jwt.io, it goes to their server. When you use an online regex tester, your test strings are logged. I built Antigravity Tools so every operation runs inside your browser, using native APIs.

No Node.js backend
No npm packages
No webpack/vite/parcel
No Google Analytics
No cookies

Everything runs on Web Crypto API, Canvas API, Web Audio API, and IndexedDB — all native to modern browsers.

The 8 tool categories

🔐 Security & Auth Tools

  • JWT Inspector — decode JWT header, payload, and check expiry locally
  • RSA & ECC Key Generator — generate 2048-bit key pairs via SubtleCrypto
  • Hash & Password Generator — SHA-256/SHA-512 via Web Crypto
  • PII Masker — strip emails, credit cards, SSNs, IPs from text
  • Universal Encoder/Decoder — Base64, URL, Hex, HTML entities, Unicode

🤖 AI & Prompting Tools

  • AI Token Counter — estimate cost across GPT-4o, Claude 3.5, Gemini 2.0, DeepSeek R1
  • System Prompt Builder — structure agent instructions with XML tags and tool definitions
  • AI Text Humanizer — rephrase robotic AI output into natural writing
  • Prompt Cost Trimmer — compress prompts by 30–50% to reduce API costs

⚡ Dev & Code Tools

  • JSON Workbench — beautify, validate, convert to TypeScript, Python, Go types
  • cURL Converter — cURL → JS fetch, Python requests, Go, PHP
  • Regex Tester — real-time match highlighting with capture group display
  • Cron Builder — visual cron expression editor with plain-English output
  • Git Command Helper — build undo/squash/cherry-pick commands visually

Try it

👉 https://antigravitytools.app

articles.title: I wrote a JavaScript framework in 2013. Here's what that world looked like
articles.description: On September 26, 2013, I made the first commit of Matreshka.js, a small framework for two-way data...
articles.body_html:
On September 26, 2013, I made the first commit of Matreshka.js, a small framework for two-way data binding. It got about 900 stars on GitHub, lived for years, and then I left it. This month I brought it back. Going through the old code felt like opening a time capsule, so here is what front-end work looked like back then.

Every new project felt like Christmas

In 2013 a new open source project was an event. Backbone.js reached 1.0 that March. AngularJS was the new hot thing, with its "magic" two-way binding. Ember reached 1.0 in August. Knockout had observables. Then, in May, Facebook showed React at JSConf US, and people laughed at JSX: HTML inside JavaScript looked like a step back.

You read the source of each new library to see how it worked. A good idea could change how everyone wrote code the next month. A blog post about a new pattern went around for weeks.

Today it is different. Something new ships every day, and an AI can write a framework in an afternoon. Nobody waits for the next release anymore. Maybe that is fine, but I miss the feeling.

You had to know every browser

"It works in Chrome" meant nothing. Internet Explorer 8 was still everywhere: on office computers, in banks, in government. jQuery 2.0 dropped IE 6, 7 and 8 in April 2013, and the jQuery team had to tell everyone to keep using the 1.x line for those browsers.

So you knew things like these by heart:

  • IE 8 had no addEventListener. It had attachEvent('onclick', …), and the event object came from window.event, with srcElement instead of target.
  • Firefox had no innerText, only textContent. Old IE had no textContent, only innerText.
  • IE 8 had no Array.prototype.indexOf, no forEach, no map, no getElementsByClassName.
  • A trailing comma in an object literal ({ a: 1, }) could break the whole script in old IE.
  • A page could switch IE into an older "Document Mode", and your code had to detect it.

Matreshka is built on getters and setters: assign app.x = 'hi' and the bound input updates. In IE 8, Object.defineProperty existed, but it only worked on DOM objects. So the 2014 Matreshka did something I still find funny. On IE 8, every instance of a Matreshka class was secretly an XDomainRequest, the IE 8 object for cross-domain requests. It is a host object, so defineProperty worked on it. The class code created one and copied the prototype methods onto it:

// IE 8 allows getters and setters only on DOM objects,
// so every instance is secretly an XDomainRequest (an AJAX object)
if (ie8) {
  constructor = function () {
    var r = new XDomainRequest;
    for (var p in constructor.prototype) if (p !== 'constructor') {
      r[p] = constructor.prototype[p];
    }
    realConstructor.apply(r, arguments);
    return r;
  };
}

That is the real code from the repository, July 2014, trimmed a little, comment added. It shipped.

Testing meant virtual machines. Microsoft gave away Windows images with each IE version, and you clicked through your app in every one of them.

You had to know JavaScript itself

There was no let and no const (they came with ES2015). There was var, and you had to know its traps.

var is hoisted:

console.log(x); // undefined, not an error
var x = 5;

var lives in the function, not in the block, so every callback in a loop sees the last value:

for (var i = 0; i < 3; i++) {
  setTimeout(function () { console.log(i); }, 0);
}
// 3 3 3

The fix was a function that runs right away (an IIFE) to capture i. Everyone wrote them.

this got lost all the time:

var user = { name: 'Ann', hi: function () { return this.name; } };
var hi = user.hi;
hi(); // not 'Ann': `this` is the global object now

So every codebase had var self = this; at the top of half the functions. IE 8 had no Function.prototype.bind either.

== had its own rules:

'' == 0    // true
'0' == 0   // true
'' == '0'  // false

And there was with, which people asked about in interviews:

var obj = { a: 1 };
with (obj) {
  a = 2; // obj.a is 2
  b = 3; // obj has no b, so this creates a global variable b
}

with was already forbidden in strict mode, but you still met it in old code and had to read it.

No npm for the front end

npm was for Node. For the browser you downloaded a file, put it in /js/vendor/, and added a <script> tag. The order of the tags mattered: jQuery first, then the plugins, then your code. Bower helped a little. Grunt ran the build: concatenate, minify, done. Gulp came out that year. Matreshka's first build was a Gruntfile.js, a week after the first commit, and the 2014 repo has a bower.json. The 2013 repo even committed its node_modules.

There were no Promises in browsers either. You had callbacks inside callbacks, or jQuery's $.Deferred.

The future that didn't come

Data binding was the big topic, and everyone thought the platform would solve it. Object.observe was going to let any object report its changes, natively, and Chrome shipped it in 2014. Frameworks planned around it. In November 2015 it was withdrawn: hardly anyone used it, and libraries had moved to getters, setters and immutable data. Matreshka was on getters and setters from the start, so it didn't miss it.

Matreshka.js today

I brought it back for the same reason you keep an old photo. But it turned out to have a real job.

Matreshka 3 is a small structural MVC framework for pages that already exist. You take HTML you already have and bind properties to it. There is no build step and no virtual DOM. One <script> tag and about 24 kB gzipped:

<input class="in" type="text">
<output class="out"></output>

<script src="https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/matreshka@3/dist/matreshka.min.js"></script>
<script>
  const app = new Matreshka();
  app.bindNode('x', '.in, .out');
  app.x = 'Hello';
</script>

Two places where this fits:

  • Legacy sites. A server-rendered page with jQuery and no build pipeline. You add structure (models, collections, bindings) without rewriting it in React.
  • Standalone HTML files written by AI. Ask an AI for a small tool or a dashboard, and you often get one HTML file. Matreshka gives that file a structure: data in models, the DOM bound to them, nothing to install.

In both cases an AI agent may be the one writing the code, so there is an agent skill. It teaches your coding agent how to use Matreshka:

npx skills add finom/matreshka

It still supports the browsers jQuery 4 supports, Internet Explorer 11 included. Some habits from 2013 stay.

Docs: matreshka.js.org · Code: github.com/finom/matreshka

articles.title: Spec-driven development in reverse: write the code, keep the receipt
articles.description: A while ago I had to make a change in a project with no SDD framework at all: no proposal, no design,...
articles.body_html:
A while ago I had to make a change in a project with no SDD framework at all: no proposal, no design, no delta specs, not even a modest tasks.md hiding in a corner. I braced myself for a long agent onboarding, an hour of wandering through the code, mixing up modules and asking where the entry point is. Instead the model just worked out the code, found the spots that needed touching, made the change, and got through the code owner's review without drama, all without a single spec.

After that I looked at my work project on OpenSpec, at its openspec/ folder with a couple hundred files in it, and had to ask: why are we generating, storing and committing a pile of artifacts that a modern model doesn't need? Who is all this paperwork for, if its main reader gets along fine without it?

That question turned into SlimSpec, a plugin for Claude Code. It keeps the parts of SDD that work and throws out the rest. On a real project a comparable change cost it 29.7M tokens versus 45.7M for OpenSpec, and not a single line of process files ended up in git. This post covers where the idea came from, how the flow works, the numbers, and the bill. Spoiler: there is a bill. There's no free lunch, even when the lunch is made of tokens.

Why we needed SDD in the first place

Not long ago models were weaker, context windows were small, and subagents didn't exist. The routine was: write a detailed plan in one session, implement it in the next. The model kept losing context, like a goldfish discovering the little castle all over again on every lap of the tank. Project memory had to live somewhere, or every session started with "hi, I'm the new junior, walk me through everything from the top."

Spec-driven development was the fix for precisely that: small context, no subagents, the need for a detailed plan. You write it all down and put the paper in the repo, and the next session reads the paper. It worked like clockwork, so it became the standard.

Around the same time, the two frameworks I'd call the big ones showed up: OpenSpec and Superpowers. I worked with both, and OpenSpec became my daily driver. What I liked about them:

  • the explore mode (Superpowers calls it brainstorming), where the design takes shape before the plan. Probably the best thing to happen to AI-assisted development so far: think first, write code second, not the other way around;
  • the plan and the specs themselves;
  • in OpenSpec's case, spec merging too: the living spec keeps only what matters. Superpowers has nothing like it and just keeps piling up design files, like the drawer of plastic bags under the kitchen sink: throwing them out feels wrong, and finding the one you need stopped being possible long ago.

All of it fit neatly into the SDD flow the community had settled on.

Where OpenSpec started to drag

In my pet projects I used OpenSpec with cheaper Chinese models for a long time and saw no problems. If anything, the opposite: code got easier to write and maintain, semantic duplicates went away (you know, when a project suddenly turns out to have three date-formatting functions), and the agent got things right more often.

Our team picked OpenSpec for a commercial project too, and at first I was all in. A couple of months later it was obvious the flow was painfully slow, especially once we dropped manual review. We had a corporate subscription and no reason to save on limits, we ran several features in parallel across a row of terminals, and the process still crawled like a DMV line for a form certifying that you already have the form.

What slowed it down:

  • After the proposal come four more artifacts: design, tasks, delta specs and the rest. We barely read them, but they were dutifully written, committed and shipped off to the archive. Did everyone get the memo about the new cover sheets? We did. Every single time.
  • Any edit to an unarchived change turns into yet another change. Changed your mind halfway through? Kindly fill out form 27B/6.
  • A rebase is mandatory before archiving. After that you have to get the agent to re-check the spec merge, because someone else may have touched the section your MODIFIED block lands in. Archive day had strong "this is fine" dog energy: coffee in hand, room on fire.

My personal bureaucracy record: I needed to remove a feature, a piece of a screen nobody needed anymore. A deletion task, what could be simpler? Delete the code, delete the tests, close the ticket. The final diff:

Almost 5,500 lines went out and almost as many came in. What came in, of course, was specs: a proposal on why we're deleting, a design on how we're deleting, tasks on what order we're deleting in, and REMOVED deltas on what exactly got deleted. To throw out 5k lines I had to write 5k lines. Yo dawg, I heard you like deleting code, so we put specs in your deletion. It's like hauling an old couch to the dump, and the dump wants a bill of sale, a condition report and a photo of every scratch first.

Then came that project with no framework, and it all clicked.

The main session is the design

I've been handing all the mechanics off to subagents for a while now. My main session has turned into a conversation: I brainstorm the feature with the agent, and the design and the plan take shape right there. Deviations from the plan get recorded in the same place without opening a new change. If a follow-up starts to grow, the agent itself suggests moving it out of scope, into non-goals. Nobody files a form. I say "let's do it differently", and that's that.

So I already have a source of truth for the feature: the session itself. "Wait, the session was the spec all along?" Always has been. Files only matter in case the session gets lost or chewed up by compaction. Think of a reserve parachute: good to have, but you don't expect to pull it on every jump. Hence "SDD in reverse": the spec doesn't drive the work, the work leaves a spec behind when it's done.

I built my own framework around that idea: take the best of what came before and make it lighter, faster and cheaper. A greatest-hits album of other people's frameworks, remastered with TDD.

How SlimSpec works

Inside there are only skills and agent definitions for Claude Code. There are no scripts, hooks or CLI, so there isn't much to break. Install and run:

/plugin marketplace add yushman/slimspec
/plugin install slimspec@slimspec

/slimspec <idea>

The whole loop in one picture:

It all starts with explore. A scanner subagent reads the module specs, then the code, and comes back with a short brief: what's here, where things live, what might break. Then the main session grills me, one question per decision, with independent questions batched together. It feels like a job interview where the candidate is your own idea, and that's useful: half of the "obvious" decisions stop looking obvious by the second question. The result goes into explore.md: goal, non-goals, decisions with rejected alternatives, risks. There's no separate proposal or design; explore is the spec of the change. The session never moves on to the plan by itself; that's my call.

In plan, the planner lays the work out in tasks.md as waves. Each wave is split into lanes of related tasks. Lanes in the same wave touch non-overlapping files, so they run in parallel. You eat an elephant one bite at a time, but if the bites are on different plates, you can eat several at once. Each task gets its first failing test written down right away.

apply is the short one: one implementer per lane works through its tasks in order and reports red and green for each. After each wave the main session runs the full test suite, so two parallel lanes don't step on each other's toes.

verify is more interesting. The reviewer checks the result against the plan and the design, and makes sure each red run failed for a real reason, not because of a typo or a forgotten import. A test that fails with ModuleNotFoundError isn't red, it's just broken. Task failed successfully. Code review is delegated to the built-in /code-review. Bugs in the code go back to apply automatically. Design questions come to me through refine: it patches explore.md and sends only the invalidated tasks back to apply, like a cashier voiding three items instead of ringing up the whole cart again. If two automatic fix rounds don't help, the session pulls me in.

ground gets its own section below, because that's where the important part is.

There are two stops: after explore and after plan. At each one the session walks me through everything in detail. After explore that's the design, with before/after diagrams and path:line references; after plan, all the waves, lanes and the test for each task. Everything else runs on its own and only pings me with questions. You can go get a coffee. You can even get a second one.

Subagents don't talk to the user

The main session makes the decisions. Subagents stay in their lane, literally: do your part, report back. What happens in the subagent stays in the subagent. The report is short and structured, without logs or diffs:

status: DONE | BLOCKED | FAILED
task: T3
files: [src/auth/token.ts, src/auth/token.test.ts]
decisions: ["used existing clock abstraction"]
deviations: ["renamed validate → verifyToken"]
tdd:
  red: "token.test.ts: rejects expired token — FAIL (expected 401, got 200)"
  green: "12 passed"
questions: []

Hit an open question? The agent stops with BLOCKED instead of guessing. The main session asks me and relaunches the agent with the answer. Its context stays free of walls of test logs, yet every decision and every outcome is in there.

TDD and review are baked into the flow

TDD and code review are table stakes by now, so I'd rather they live in the framework than in somebody's self-discipline. Discipline, as we all know, runs out on Friday evening. TDD is enforced by evidence rather than a hook: verify won't accept a task without a red run. You shall not pass! (Gandalf, part-time reviewer.) Where TDD doesn't apply (config, styles, migrations), the task is marked test: none — <reason> with an alternative check, and all such exemptions are shown at the plan gate. You can't sneak an "oh, no tests needed here" into the middle of the list.

Two temporary files

A change lives in .slimspec/changes/<slug>/ as explore.md and tasks.md. SlimSpec adds the folder to .gitignore itself and deletes it after ground. No eulogy, and none needed: by then everything useful in it has already moved into the specs. History lives in the commits and the updated specs. Lost the session? /slimspec <slug> picks up where you left off.

Grounding: the only thing left of SDD

The last step, ground, is probably the only thing SlimSpec still has in common with classic SDD.

Durable knowledge gets distilled from the change: behavior, invariants, contracts, decisions. The plan and the process get thrown out, Marie Kondo style, after you thank them for their service. Who's going to care in six months that task T3 was in the second wave? Nobody. The distilled knowledge is then merged into the module spec. Phil Karlton said there are only two hard things in computer science; he never had to merge delta specs. Here's the main difference from OpenSpec: instead of ADDED/MODIFIED/REMOVED blocks, the merge is done by an agent that understands why the change was made and how it's designed. If the change contradicts something the spec says, that statement gets rewritten instead of getting a new one appended next to it. Otherwise the spec quickly turns into "it used to be like this, but then it became like that, although see item 7". Finally, the agent checks that the updated spec covers the change's goal and doesn't contradict the decisions that were made.

The result goes into the nested CLAUDE.md of the relevant module. Claude Code loads these files on its own whenever it works in that directory, so the spec ends up in context for free, right where it's needed. One spec per module instead of a scatter of per-capability files. No need to remember which spec to feed the agent: it walks into the module, and the spec is already there.

The numbers

I moved two of my projects to SlimSpec. The measurements come from one of them, looqlog, a log viewer in Rust with a web UI. It used to live on OpenSpec and moved over with /slimspec:migrate-openspec.

Migration

We had 23 spec files, 23 archived changes, 200 files in openspec/ and 733 KB of history. Not that the agent needed all of that for the trip, but once you start collecting artifacts, it gets hard to stop.

OpenSpec SlimSpec
Behavior specs 23 files, 2,941 lines, ~155 KB 3 files, 484 lines, ~34 KB
Change archive 23 changes, 12,394 lines, ~733 KB 0
Root CLAUDE.md 130 lines 121 lines
Files in openspec/ 200 0

WHEN/THEN scenarios were folded into the requirements they described. Empty Purpose sections and boilerplate SHALLs are gone (SHALL, SHALL NOT, SHALL ALWAYS... the specs read like an army field manual). The agent reads only the spec of the module it's working in: an edit in web/ pulls in ~11 KB, not capability files from all over the tree. Four SlimSpec changes later, the module specs have grown to 4 files and 641 lines. That's still 78% less than OpenSpec had, and the growth tracks the code, not the paperwork.

What one change costs

I counted from Claude Code transcripts. Tokens here mean all the input the model processed (input + cache read + cache write), main session and subagents together. The closest pair in size:

OpenSpec (logcat-padded-tags) SlimSpec full (iana-tz-hash)
Code changed 409 lines, 4 files, 1 module 435 lines, 15 files, 3 modules
Tokens processed 45.7M 29.7M (−35%)
Tokens per line of code ~110k ~68k (−38%)
Review none 2 verify rounds at depth high, one real blocker fixed
Process files committed ~530 lines 0
Time, gates included 91 min 56 min

And SlimSpec did more work in that run: 5 decision questions, 3 gates, 9 tasks in 3 waves, ground into 4 specs, an ADR and both READMEs. The blocker the reviewer found was a panic on extreme dates, the kind of bug that shows up in prod at exactly 11:59 PM on December 31st. The OpenSpec run had no review at all.

Small changes tell the same story. Two OpenSpec changes processed 31.5M and 45.7M tokens, two SlimSpec ones (fast and medium) 6.8M and 12.5M. A single OpenSpec implementer chewed through 13–16M tokens on its own; a SlimSpec subagent, 0–1M. Each one gets a single narrow lane and doesn't have to read the whole world to change one function.

Now the caveats, which I'd rather name myself before the comments do. n = 1–2 per approach, one project. The plural of anecdote isn't data, and I barely have the plural. The small SlimSpec changes were 5–10× smaller in code, so part of the gap is just size. Some SlimSpec agents ran on Sonnet or Haiku. On the other hand, the main session of the full run was dragging along unrelated context from earlier work, which inflates its count. So treat the numbers as an observation rather than a benchmark, though a hard one to ignore.

What didn't work along the way

It all looked great on paper. Some things I built one way first and then had to redo.

An implementer per task. It looked beautiful: a fresh agent, a narrow context, everything neat and tidy. In practice every cold start re-read explore.md, the specs and the code. Every task meant another round of "hi, so what's this project about?". 50 First Dates, with tokens on the meter. Now one implementer runs a lane of related tasks.

Worktrees for isolation in full mode. That didn't fly: a subagent's worktree branches off the last commit and can't see the uncommitted results of earlier waves. The second wave was building the second floor of a house with no first floor. I'd have had to commit after every wave. Instead I kept parallelism over non-overlapping files in a single working tree.

I wanted a hook that wouldn't let you edit code without a failing test. Sounds strict and reliable. But a prompt hook can't verify that a red run actually happened, and plugin hooks are always on, whatever the mode. A security guard who can't check badges, posted at every door. The check moved into verify.

Setup had its own comedy moment. First I wrote a bash wizard: menus, prompts, the works. Textbook yak shaving. Then it turned out a skill can't drive an interactive script, and ! in the session runs without a TTY. The wizard was pretty, it just couldn't be launched. Now /slimspec:init simply asks its questions right in the session.

And one small thing that annoyed me every day: in explore, questions came strictly one at a time. You waited a full round trip per decision, even when all the questions were known upfront. Very "your call is important to us, please stay on the line". Now independent ones come in a batch, up to four at a time.

What it cost

Here's the receipt, everything that went out the door along with the extra artifacts:

  • Scenarios as a ready-made list of test cases are gone.
  • Rationale for individual changes is partly lost. Some of it survived in ADRs, the rest lives only in git history. If you enjoy archaeology with git log, you'll love it.
  • The largest module spec (~14 KB) is loaded whole for any work in that module.
  • It only works with Claude Code. OpenSpec supports 30+ AI tools; Superpowers also works with many agents and does a bunch of things beyond specs: debugging, worktrees, review. SlimSpec only covers the spec-driven loop and doesn't pretend to be a Swiss Army knife.

Tuning it for your project

Config is optional, and every key has a default. Don't want to configure anything? Then don't; it'll run as is. /slimspec:init asks everything in the session and writes .slimspec/config.yaml:

mode: medium              # fast | medium | full
spec:
  format: claude-md       # claude-md | readme | central | native | none
  unit: auto              # auto (by build files) | dir glob, e.g. "src/*/"
  adr: false              # also keep decisions in docs/adr/NNNN-*.md
test: auto                # or an explicit command
commit: none              # none | lane | wave
apply:
  agents: 3               # max parallel implementers
review:
  depth: auto             # auto (by mode) | low | medium | high
models: {}                # per-role models: scanner, planner, implementer, reviewer, grounder

mode sets how heavy the loop is. In fast, explore and plan share one file, and you get at most three questions, one implementer and review at low. That's for "change the button text without losing your mind". medium adds the scanner, grilling, the planner and parallel lanes, with review at medium. full adds an explicit gate on explore.md and review at high, for changes you'd still like to sleep at night after. You don't even have to pick: after the scan, /slimspec suggests a mode based on the size of the change.

spec.format decides where specs live. The default is nested CLAUDE.md files. You can also use a README.md next to the code, a shared specs/ folder for features that cut across modules, the language's native docs (Go doc.go, Rust //!, Python docstrings, KDoc), or none, in which case ground is skipped. That one's for the "the code is the documentation" crowd.

spec.unit says what counts as a module; auto finds the boundaries from package.json, go.mod, Cargo.toml, build.gradle(.kts), pyproject.toml.

commit turns on a commit after each lane or wave. Only the main session commits, agents never do. SlimSpec can't push at all, and that's a feature: no surprises in main at 3 AM.

models assigns a model per role. By default the scanner and implementer run on Sonnet, and the planner, reviewer and grounder on Opus. Thinking is expensive and doing is cheaper; that's the whole economics of it.

If your project already runs on OpenSpec or Superpowers, there's /slimspec:migrate-openspec and /slimspec:migrate-superpowers. Only specs are carried over: each one is mapped to modules, compressed and checked against the code. Where the code and the spec disagree, you decide, because sometimes the spec lies and sometimes the code does, and guessing isn't an option. Old files are deleted only after you confirm.

Bottom line

Strong models don't need heavy specs. Tell them what to do and where to look, and they'll reconstruct the rest from the code faster than they could read four artifacts. The tokens that go into a proposal nobody will open are better spent on the next feature, or better yet, on a new project. A million tokens here, a million there, and pretty soon it adds up to that pet project that's been sitting on the "someday" list for ages.

If a slow SDD flow is grinding you down too, try SlimSpec on a single change and compare it with your current process. I'm especially curious how it holds up in a team and on projects bigger than mine. Leave a comment or open an issue. Roasts are welcome too, just bring numbers.

articles.title: Your First Claude Code Mod: Block Edits Outside the Task's Worktree in 30 Lines
articles.description: Claude Code mods run your JavaScript on every tool call. Build a 30-line mod that refuses Edit and Write outside the task's worktree, then test it.
articles.body_html:
• Book: TypeScript Essentials
  • Also by me: The TypeScript Library — the 5-book collection
  • My project: Hermes IDE | GitHub — an IDE for developers who ship with Claude Code and other AI coding tools
  • Me: xgabriel.com | GitHub

Your agent is working in a git worktree, on its own branch, in a folder next to your main checkout. Then a stack trace from your dev server lands in its context. Every path in that trace points at the main checkout, one directory over. The agent opens ../app/src/config.ts, fixes the bug there, and your "isolated" task has just edited the copy you were using.

Worktrees keep agents apart on disk. They don't stop an agent from writing to a path outside its own folder. In Claude Code's acceptEdits mode, edits outside the working directory still ask you first, but bypassPermissions skips the prompts, and a prompt you approve at the end of a long day is still an approval.

Claude Code v2.1.287 and later can run mods: plugins whose JavaScript or TypeScript handlers run inside Claude Code when an event fires, such as a tool call. A handler can watch the event, change it, or answer it in Claude Code's place. This post builds one that answers Edit and Write calls aimed outside the session's folder with a refusal. It is 30 lines of JavaScript, plus two small JSON files.

What a mod is

A mod is a plugin with three files, laid out the way the create-a-mod tutorial lays out its own:

worktree-guard/
├── .claude-plugin/
│   └── plugin.json
└── hooks/
    ├── hooks.json
    └── register.js

plugin.json is the plugin manifest. hooks.json points to your code, and its modules key is what makes the plugin a mod. register.js is the code, which the docs call the hooks module. You don't need Node.js or a build step, because Claude Code loads .js and .ts files directly.

When the mod loads, Claude Code calls the register function the file exports and passes it a function named on. Each on call registers a hook for one event. Every hook gets three arguments: $ (the mods API), e (the event, frozen), and next (the rest of the chain, ending in Claude Code's own behaviour). Return next(e) and the tool runs. Return something else without calling next, and you have answered the event yourself.


The worktree is the plot. The mod is the gate.

Write the guard

Create the directories:

mkdir -p worktree-guard/.claude-plugin \
  worktree-guard/hooks worktree-guard/tests

Save the manifest as worktree-guard/.claude-plugin/plugin.json. Don't start the name with claude-: claude plugin validate fails names that look like Anthropic's own.

{
  "name": "worktree-guard",
  "version": "0.1.0",
  "description": "Refuses Edit and Write outside the session root"
}

Save the pointer to your code as worktree-guard/hooks/hooks.json. The path is relative to this file:

{
  "description": "worktree-guard hooks module",
  "modules": ["./register.js"]
}

And the guard itself, worktree-guard/hooks/register.js:

// Refuse Edit/Write outside the session's project root
function normalize(p) {
  const out = []
  for (const part of p.split('/')) {
    if (part === '..') out.pop()
    else if (part && part !== '.') out.push(part)
  }
  return '/' + out.join('/')
}

function isInside(root, file) {
  const r = normalize(root)
  const f = normalize(file.startsWith('/') ? file : r + '/' + file)
  return f === r || f.startsWith(r + '/')
}

async function guard($, e, next) {
  const root = await $.session.root()
  if (isInside(root, e.file_path)) return next(e)
  return { deny: `${e.file_path} is outside ${root}. ` +
    'Edit files in this worktree, or ask the user first.' }
}

export function register(on) {
  on('tool.call', { tool: ['Edit', 'Write'] }, guard)
    .catch(async ($, e, next) => {
      if (next.called) return next(e)
      return { deny: 'worktree-guard failed: ' + next.error.kind }
    })
}

{ tool: ['Edit', 'Write'] } is the matcher, a filter. An array matches any value in it, so the hook runs for those two tools only. Both carry their target as e.file_path, the field the events guide reads in its own Edit/Write example.

For the root, the mods API has both $.session.cwd() and $.session.root(). The type declarations describe root() as where the session started, or where /cd or a worktree move took it, and say a shell cd during the session does not move it. That is the boundary you want: start Claude Code in a worktree and the root is that worktree.

The hooks module has no Node.js APIs, so there is no path module to lean on (API docs). normalize folds ., .. and doubled slashes by hand, so /work/app/../main/x.ts becomes /work/main/x.ts before the comparison. The r + '/' in the prefix test stops /work/app-old from passing as a child of /work/app.

Returning { deny } without calling next means the tool never runs and no permission prompt appears. Claude reads the deny text as the tool's result, so write it as an instruction. Claude Code runs its permission check inside next, so the refusal holds in every permission mode, bypassPermissions included.

A hook that throws or times out is skipped, and the edit would go through. The .catch handler makes the guard fail closed: if guard failed before calling next, the edit is refused. The handler has a one-second limit of its own (reference), and if it fails too, the hook is skipped.

Load it and check what it touches

Load the directory for one session, without installing anything:

claude --plugin-dir ./worktree-guard

Type /plugin at the prompt. The overview says a dim line under the tabs gives the count and the names of loaded mods, so this one should read 1 mod active · worktree-guard. If the name is missing, the module didn't load.

Ask Claude to change a file one level up, for example add a comment to the top of ../README.md. The call should come back refused, with your message as the result. An edit inside the folder goes through as usual. Claude Code hot-reloads a --plugin-dir mod when you save a file in it, so you can tweak the deny text without restarting.

Before you share a mod, or install someone else's, read it the way Claude Code does:

claude plugin validate ./worktree-guard

validate runs the same static analysis Claude Code runs at load time, without executing your code. Look at three lines. The hooks: line should list tool.call with its tool filter in braces. The calls: line should list $.session.root and nothing else: no $.fs, no $.process, no $.http. And because this hook can refuse an action, validate prints a gating-hook line saying whether it has a .catch handler. This one does.

That calls: line is your audit. Mods aren't sandboxed: they run with your permissions and can read files, start processes and make network requests through the mods API.

Test it without a session

claude plugin test runs any *.test.ts file in the plugin directory with no session, sign-in or network (test docs). Nothing real answers in a test, so you stub the session root and the tool itself. Save this as worktree-guard/tests/guard.test.ts:

import { expect, test } from 'claude-code/testing'

test('refuses a write outside the root', async ($, on) => {
  on('session.root', () => ({ value: '/work/app' }))
  on('tool.call', () => ({ result: 'ok' }))
  const out = await $.tool.call({
    tool: 'Write',
    file_path: '/work/app/../main/x.ts',
    content: '',
  })
  expect(out.deny).toBeDefined()
})

test('lets an edit inside the root through', async ($, on) => {
  on('session.root', () => ({ value: '/work/app' }))
  on('tool.call', () => ({ result: 'ok' }))
  const out = await $.tool.call({
    tool: 'Edit',
    file_path: '/work/app/src/a.ts',
    old_string: 'a',
    new_string: 'b',
  })
  expect(out).toEqual({ result: 'ok' })
})

A stub for a mods API call is named without the $. and returns { value }. The tool.call stub stands in for Claude Code running the tool, so a call the guard lets through resolves to { result: 'ok' }. Run claude plugin test from the worktree-guard directory; it exits with status 1 on a failure, so it fits in CI. I haven't run this suite myself, so if a field name disagrees with your build, trust the declarations Claude Code writes into .claude-plugin/types/.

Every Hermes task, guarded

The guard gets more useful when every task already has a worktree. I build Hermes IDE, so weigh this section with that in mind. In Hermes, ⌘N (Ctrl+Shift+N on Windows and Linux) starts each task on its own hermes/<name> branch, in its own worktree, with the task as the agent's first prompt. Claude Code runs there as the regular CLI in a real terminal, so a Claude Code session in a Hermes task starts with its root at that task's worktree.


The ⌘N New task sheet in Hermes 2.3.4: Claude Code, the orders-api project, a new hermes/ worktree, Accept edits, and a preview of the claude command Hermes will run.

You can't add --plugin-dir to a command you don't type yourself. For that case Claude Code reads CLAUDE_CODE_PLUGIN_DIRS, an environment variable the reference describes as plugin directories "for apps you can't pass a flag to". It takes absolute paths and can live in the env block of ~/.claude/settings.json:

{
  "env": {
    "CLAUDE_CODE_PLUGIN_DIRS": "/path/to/mods/worktree-guard"
  }
}

Put the mod somewhere outside your repositories, so no task can rewrite the guard through Edit or Write. From then on, every normal Claude Code session loads the mod, wherever it was started, and an Edit or Write aimed outside the folder Hermes made for the task comes back refused.


The Review Desk's Worktrees tab: one Hermes worktree each for orders-api, web-app and orders-types, with each one's hermes/ branch, task, age and disk size.

One interaction to know about. Since Hermes 2.3.0, a task can include up to 5 extra folders, and those are worked on where they are, on their current branch, not in the task's worktree. The guard will refuse Claude's edits in them. If you use extra folders, add their paths to an allow list in isInside, or leave the guard off for those tasks.

What this mod doesn't stop

It guards two tools by path. It is not a sandbox.

  • Bash. sed -i, cp or echo > into ../app never goes through Edit or Write. Outside bypassPermissions, Claude Code checks output redirects and tee targets against the working directories and asks first. Its sandboxing isolates the Bash commands Claude runs.
  • Other writers. NotebookEdit and MCP tools that write files carry their paths in other fields. Add them to the matcher with the field each one uses.
  • Symlinks. The check compares path strings. A symlink inside the worktree that points outside it passes.
  • Subagents. tool.call fires for subagent calls too. I haven't checked what $.session.root() returns inside a subagent that runs in its own worktree, so test that before you rely on it.
  • POSIX paths only. normalize splits on /. On Windows you would need to handle drive letters and backslashes.

If you'd rather not write JavaScript, a PreToolUse settings hook running a script you already have can block the same calls, and the docs' comparison table recommends exactly that case for settings hooks. What the mod adds is claude plugin test and a validate report anyone can read before loading it.

If this was useful

The hooks module is a plain ES module of async functions, and once you rename it to register.ts and point modules at the new name, the declarations Claude Code writes into .claude-plugin/types/ narrow e as soon as you check e.tool. That is the everyday TypeScript in TypeScript Essentials: types, narrowing, modules and async, across Node, Bun, Deno and the browser. If you write mods, it's the book that makes those type files read like documentation.

  • TypeScript Essentials — types, narrowing, modules, async, daily-driver tooling
  • The TypeScript Type System — generics, mapped/conditional types, infer, template literals, branded types
  • Kotlin and Java to TypeScript — JVM developers moving to TypeScript
  • PHP to TypeScript — PHP 8+ developers moving to TypeScript
  • TypeScript in Production — tsconfig, build tools, monorepos, library authoring, dual ESM/CJS, JSR

Start with books 1 and 2. Coming from Kotlin or Java, take book 3 in place of book 1; coming from PHP, book 4. If you ship TypeScript at work, add book 5.

Hermes IDE is free, source-available under BSL 1.1, on macOS, Windows and Linux, and not affiliated with Anthropic or any agent vendor: download it or star it on GitHub.

All five books ship in ebook, paperback, and hardcover.

articles.title: I Built a Photorealistic AI Virtual Try-On App Entirely on a $150 Phone (And How We Pivoted When It Failed)
articles.description: Most people think you need a MacBook, cloud credits, and a team of engineers to build a generative AI...
articles.body_html:
Most people think you need a MacBook, cloud credits, and a team of engineers to build a generative AI product.

My co-founder Akhouri (13) and I (12) just proved that wrong. We built and launched ACA, a privacy-first virtual try-on app, entirely using a $150 Android phone, Termux, and pure stubbornness.

But we almost didn't make it. Here is the story of our pivot.

Phase 1: The Illusion of Path A

We started by trying to run Virtual Try-On (VTON) entirely in the browser. We used MoveNet (TensorFlow.js) to extract skeletal keypoints and Barycentric Triangle Warping to stretch a 2D garment image over the user's body.

It was a disaster.
Akhouri ran 54 systematic tests and 13 alternative approaches. Every single one failed. The fabric didn't bend, the shadows didn't match, and it looked like a paper cutout floating in the air.

My co-founder sent me a message: "ACA is hard or impossible in this case. All paths are impossible."

Phase 2: The Termux Trenches

I refused to give up. 86.6% of people don't use virtual try-on because they don't trust companies with their photos. We had to solve this.

I tried to build a local Trusted Execution Environment in Termux. What followed was a week of pure technical hell:

  • Hit No matching distribution found trying to install MediaPipe.
  • Node.js threw Cannot find module 'glob', breaking npm entirely.
  • Google Cloud slammed a 13+ age verification wall in my face.
  • I was debugging blind on a 4-inch screen with no Chrome DevTools.

Phase 3: The Pivot (Split Inference)

We realized trying to force a massive diffusion model onto a POCO C55 was like fitting a V8 engine into a bicycle.

So, we pivoted to a Split Inference Architecture:

  1. The phone handles the UI (Vanilla JS, 60fps Canvas).
  2. Supabase handles Auth and strict Row-Level Security (RLS).
  3. The cloud handles the heavy lifting via the IDM-VTON Diffusion Model (using the @gradio/client to bypass CORS and join the Hugging Face GPU queue via WebSockets).

The Magic Moment

I fixed the image extraction logic. I uploaded a photo and a clean polo shirt. I hit generate.

The progress bar said: In Queue... waiting for GPU...
I waited 60 seconds.

Then, the log flashed: ✔ AI Generation Complete!

The canvas rendered. The AI had generated fabric folds, shadows, and perfect lighting matching the background. Not a sticker. Not a warp. Photorealistic.

We literally screamed. We did it.

Here is the exact output from that session:

(1. The Garment Input)

(2. The Original User Photo)

(3. The ACA Generated Output)

A Note on Privacy: You'll notice the faces in our test images are blurred. This isn't a bug; it's a feature. ACA is built on a strict privacy-first philosophy. We don't harvest biometric data, and we don't train our models on our users' faces. Even when testing our own app with family, we protect their identities. When you use ACA, your face belongs to you, not our servers.

The Reality of v1.0

We are live at https://aca-vto.netlify.app/.

Is it perfect? No.

  • The Hugging Face token is currently baked into the client-side JS (it's read-only, but a Cloudflare Worker proxy is scheduled for v1.1).
  • Free public GPUs mean a 20-40s wait time.

But it works. It’s a fully functional SaaS product with authentication, database persistence, and generative AI, built with zero budget and deployed entirely from a mobile phone.

To anyone who says you need expensive hardware to build AI: you don't. You need a terminal, and the stubbornness to keep going when the code says "impossible."

We are just getting started. 🐯🚀

(Shoutout to the HYNAWEB engineering team: Akhouri Anmol Kumar, CTO)

articles.title: Screenshot Every Page of a Website from Its Sitemap with One Node.js Script
articles.description: Read every URL from a sitemap, capture each page at desktop and mobile widths in real Chrome, and save named PNGs, a CSV manifest and a contact sheet with one Node.js script.
articles.body_html:
You're about to relaunch a site and someone asks for a screenshot of every page as it stands today. Or a client wants to sign off 140 pages of copy, or legal wants a dated record of what the pricing page said. Doing it by hand means opening each URL, waiting for the lazy images, closing the cookie banner and saving the file under a name you'll still understand next month. Two minutes a page adds up to most of a working day for a 200-page site.

So I wrote one Node.js script that reads the sitemap, captures every page at desktop and mobile widths in real Chrome, and leaves a folder of named PNGs, a CSV manifest and a contact sheet. Last run: 38 full-page captures in 35 seconds, no failures.

Disclosure: I run HTML to Image, and the script uses its Screenshot API for the captures. This is a cross-post of the full guide on the HTML to Image blog, which is the canonical version and goes further into webhooks, costs and compliance archives.

Prerequisites

  • Node.js 18 or later, for the built-in fetch.
  • An HTML to Image API key. The free credits are enough to try this on a handful of pages.
  • A site with a sitemap, or a text file of URLs from a crawl. 
npm install @html2img/client
export HTML2IMG_API_KEY=your_api_key

Step 1: Find the sitemap

Most sites declare their sitemap in robots.txt, so check there first:

curl -s https://example.com/robots.txt | grep -i '^sitemap:'

If nothing comes back, try /sitemap.xml, then /sitemap_index.xml (Yoast and Rank Math on WordPress), then /wp-sitemap.xml (WordPress core since 5.5). Big sites use a sitemap index that points at child sitemaps, some of them gzipped. The script follows all of that, so you only ever pass the top-level URL.

One caveat: a sitemap is the list the CMS chooses to publish. Orphaned landing pages and anything marked noindex won't be in it. For a migration archive, cross-check against a crawl and feed the script a text file instead.

Step 2: The script

Save this as capture-site.mjs. It's long-ish because it handles the boring parts properly: sitemap indexes, .gz files, duplicates, a credit check before spending anything, four captures at a time, retries for errors that can recover, and the reports at the end.

// capture-site.mjs
// node capture-site.mjs https://example.com/sitemap.xml [--dry-run]
// node capture-site.mjs urls.txt
import { mkdir, readFile, writeFile } from 'node:fs/promises';
import { gunzipSync } from 'node:zlib';
import {
  Html2img,
  InsufficientCreditsError,
  TimeoutError,
  ServerError,
  ConnectionError,
} from '@html2img/client';

const SOURCE = process.argv[2];
const DRY_RUN = process.argv.includes('--dry-run');
const OUT = 'shots';
const CONCURRENCY = 4;
const MAX_ATTEMPTS = 3;

// One credit per page per variant.
const VARIANTS = [
  { name: 'desktop', width: 1440 },
  { name: 'mobile', width: 390 },
  // { name: 'pdf', format: 'pdf' }, // A4 document with a real text layer
];

// Sent with every capture.
const CAPTURE = {
  fullpage: true,
  css: `#onetrust-banner-sdk, .onetrust-pc-dark-filter, #CybotCookiebotDialog,
        .qc-cmp2-container, .osano-cm-window, #cookie-law-info-bar,
        .intercom-frame, #crisp-chatbox { display: none !important; }`,
};

const SKIP = /\.(pdf|jpe?g|png|gif|webp|svg|zip|mp4|xml)$/i;
const apiKey = process.env.HTML2IMG_API_KEY;
const client = DRY_RUN ? null : new Html2img(apiKey);

// 1. Every <loc> in a sitemap, following sitemap indexes and .gz files.
async function readSitemap(url, seen = new Set()) {
  if (seen.has(url)) return [];
  seen.add(url);
  const res = await fetch(url);
  if (!res.ok) throw new Error(`${url} returned ${res.status}`);
  let body = Buffer.from(await res.arrayBuffer());
  if (body[0] === 0x1f && body[1] === 0x8b) body = gunzipSync(body);
  const xml = body.toString('utf8');
  const locs = [...xml.matchAll(/<loc>\s*(?:<!\[CDATA\[)?(.*?)(?:\]\]>)?\s*<\/loc>/gs)]
    .map((m) => m[1].replace(/&(amp|apos|quot|lt|gt);/g, (_, e) =>
      ({ amp: '&', apos: "'", quot: '"', lt: '<', gt: '>' })[e]));
  if (!/<sitemapindex[\s>]/.test(xml)) return locs;
  const children = await Promise.all(locs.map((loc) => readSitemap(loc, seen)));
  return children.flat();
}

// 2. Same site only, no files, no duplicates.
const bare = (host) => host.replace(/^www\./, '');
function toPages(urls, onlyHost) {
  const pages = new Set();
  for (const raw of urls) {
    let u;
    try { u = new URL(raw.trim()); } catch { continue; } // header rows, blanks
    if (onlyHost && bare(u.hostname) !== bare(onlyHost)) continue;
    if (SKIP.test(u.pathname)) continue;
    u.hash = '';
    pages.add(u.href);
  }
  return [...pages];
}

// "/blog/launch-notes/" -> "blog__launch-notes"
let multiSite = false;
function fileName(page) {
  const { hostname, pathname, search } = new URL(page);
  const slug = (pathname + search)
    .replace(/^\/+|\/+$/g, '')
    .split('/')
    .map((part) => part.replace(/[^a-z0-9]+/gi, '-').replace(/^-|-$/g, ''))
    .join('__')
    .toLowerCase()
    .slice(0, 150) || 'home';
  return multiSite ? `${bare(hostname)}__${slug}` : slug;
}

async function creditsLeft() {
  const res = await fetch('https://app.html2img.com/api/me', {
    headers: { 'X-API-Key': apiKey },
  });
  if (!res.ok) throw new Error(`Key check failed with ${res.status}`);
  return (await res.json()).credits_remaining;
}

const retryable = (err) =>
  err instanceof TimeoutError ||
  err instanceof ServerError ||
  err instanceof ConnectionError ||
  err.errorCode === 'page_load_timeout';

// 3. One capture, retried on errors that are worth a second attempt.
async function capture({ page, variant }) {
  const { name, ...options } = variant;
  const ext = options.format === 'pdf' ? 'pdf' : 'png';
  const row = { page, variant: name, status: 'failed', file: '', image_url: '', error: '' };
  for (let attempt = 1; attempt <= MAX_ATTEMPTS; attempt++) {
    try {
      const shot = await client.screenshot({ url: page, ...CAPTURE, ...options });
      row.image_url = shot.url;
      const img = await fetch(shot.url);
      if (!img.ok) throw new Error(`download returned ${img.status}`);
      row.file = `${name}/${fileName(page)}.${ext}`;
      await writeFile(`${OUT}/${row.file}`, Buffer.from(await img.arrayBuffer()));
      return { ...row, status: 'ok', error: '' };
    } catch (err) {
      if (err instanceof InsufficientCreditsError) throw err;
      row.error = err.errorCode ?? err.message;
      if (!retryable(err) || attempt === MAX_ATTEMPTS) return row;
      await new Promise((resolve) => setTimeout(resolve, 3000 * attempt));
    }
  }
}

// 4. A fixed number of captures in flight at once.
async function runAll(jobs) {
  const rows = [];
  let next = 0;
  let stopped = false;
  async function lane() {
    while (!stopped && next < jobs.length) {
      const job = jobs[next++];
      try {
        const row = await capture(job);
        rows.push(row);
        console.log(`${rows.length}/${jobs.length} ${row.status} ${row.variant} ${job.page}`);
      } catch (err) {
        if (!stopped) console.error(`Stopping early: ${err.message}`);
        stopped = true;
      }
    }
  }
  await Promise.all(Array.from({ length: CONCURRENCY }, lane));
  return rows;
}

// 5. A manifest for spreadsheets and an index.html for people.
async function writeReports(rows) {
  const cols = ['page', 'variant', 'status', 'file', 'image_url', 'error'];
  const cell = (v) => `"${String(v).replaceAll('"', '""')}"`;
  const csv = [cols, ...rows.map((r) => cols.map((c) => r[c]))]
    .map((line) => line.map(cell).join(','))
    .join('\n');
  await writeFile(`${OUT}/manifest.csv`, csv);

  const esc = (s) => s.replace(/[&<>"]/g, (c) => `&#${c.charCodeAt(0)};`);
  const cards = rows
    .filter((r) => r.status === 'ok' && r.file.endsWith('.png'))
    .map((r) => `<a href="${esc(r.file)}"><img src="${esc(r.file)}" loading="lazy"><span>${r.variant} · ${esc(r.page)}</span></a>`)
    .join('\n');
  await writeFile(`${OUT}/index.html`, `<!doctype html><meta charset="utf-8"><title>Site capture</title>
<style>body{font:14px system-ui;margin:24px;display:grid;grid-template-columns:repeat(auto-fill,minmax(240px,1fr));gap:20px}
a{color:#334155;text-decoration:none}img{width:100%;height:320px;object-fit:cover;object-position:top;border:1px solid #e2e6ec;border-radius:8px}
span{display:block;margin-top:6px;word-break:break-all}</style>\n${cards}`);
}

const fromSitemap = /^https?:\/\//.test(SOURCE);
const urls = fromSitemap
  ? await readSitemap(SOURCE)
  : (await readFile(SOURCE, 'utf8')).split(/\r?\n/);
const pages = toPages(urls, fromSitemap ? new URL(SOURCE).hostname : null);
multiSite = new Set(pages.map((page) => bare(new URL(page).hostname))).size > 1;

if (DRY_RUN) {
  console.log(pages.join('\n'));
  process.exit(0);
}

const jobs = pages.flatMap((page) => VARIANTS.map((variant) => ({ page, variant })));
const credits = await creditsLeft();
console.log(`${pages.length} pages x ${VARIANTS.length} variants = ${jobs.length} credits. Balance: ${credits}.`);
if (credits < jobs.length) {
  console.error('Not enough credits for the whole run. Trim the list or top up first.');
  process.exit(1);
}

for (const { name } of VARIANTS) await mkdir(`${OUT}/${name}`, { recursive: true });
const rows = await runAll(jobs);
await writeReports(rows);

const failed = rows.filter((r) => r.status !== 'ok').length;
const skipped = jobs.length - rows.length;
console.log(`Saved ${rows.length - failed}, failed ${failed}, skipped ${skipped}. Open ${OUT}/index.html`);

The css string is doing quiet but important work. The renderer arrives as a first-time visitor with no cookies, so every page shows its consent banner. Injecting display: none !important for the common consent providers and chat widgets takes them out before the shot. If a site uses something else, find the banner's ID in dev tools and add it.

Step 3: Dry run first, then capture

--dry-run prints the URLs the script would capture. It doesn't need a key and spends nothing, so use it to filter out tag archives, paginated listings and anything else you don't need a picture of:

node capture-site.mjs https://html2img.com/sitemap.xml --dry-run | grep '/tools/' > urls.txt
node capture-site.mjs urls.txt

That's the real run I mentioned at the top, against the free tools section of my own site:

19 pages x 2 variants = 38 credits. Balance: 100.
1/38 ok desktop https://html2img.com/docs/mcp/tools/
2/38 ok mobile https://html2img.com/docs/mcp/tools/
3/38 ok desktop https://html2img.com/tools/
4/38 ok mobile https://html2img.com/tools/
...
38/38 ok desktop https://html2img.com/tools/youtube-thumbnail/
Saved 38, failed 0, skipped 0. Open shots/index.html

Spot the first line. My lazy grep also matched /docs/mcp/tools/, which I never meant to include. That's exactly why the dry run exists: grep '^https://html2img.com/tools/' would have kept it out.

The desktop captures came back 1,440 pixels wide and between 3,737 and 10,016 pixels tall. Here's the index.html the run produced, each card cropped to the top of its page:

What the script does when things go wrong

Not every page cooperates, so the retry logic only retries what a second attempt can fix:

  • 504 timeouts, 500s, slow-loading sites and dropped connections get two more attempts, 3 then 6 seconds apart.
  • Dead links, SSL failures and sites that block automated visitors (url_not_found, url_unreachable, connection_refused) are logged in manifest.csv and skipped.
  • Running out of credits stops every lane, still writes the reports, and tells you how many captures were skipped.

To re-run only the failures, pull them out of the manifest and run them in a fresh folder so the first run's reports stay intact:

awk -F'","' '$3 == "failed" { print substr($1, 2) }' shots/manifest.csv | sort -u > retry.txt
mkdir retry && cd retry && node ../capture-site.mjs ../retry.txt

Keep CONCURRENCY low for sites you don't own. Every capture is a real page load against somebody's production server.

A few limits worth planning around

  • Public pages only. The renderer has no cookies or headers, so anything behind a login captures as the sign-in page.
  • Infinite scroll has no bottom. Cap the feed with injected CSS such as main.feed { max-height: 12000px; overflow: hidden; }.
  • Closed accordions stay closed. Nobody clicks during a capture, so open hidden panels with CSS if they matter.
  • One credit per page per width. Desktop plus mobile doubles the cost, and the PDF variant adds a third.

Where I'd use this

Before a migration, so you have the old site on disk the day the DNS switches. For client sign-off, where one contact sheet beats 200 links. And for compliance, where the commented-out pdf variant gives you searchable A4 documents in a dated folder.

The full guide on the HTML to Image blog also covers handing long captures to a webhook instead of waiting on them, a bash version for short URL lists, and what a full-site capture costs at different sizes.

How are you archiving sites before a relaunch at the moment? Browser extension, Screaming Frog, something homegrown? Let me know in the comments.

articles.title: How to encrypt user data in the browser with the Web Crypto API
articles.description: When someone saves a note in your app, it usually travels to your server over HTTPS and then sits in...
articles.body_html:
When someone saves a note in your app, it usually travels to your server over HTTPS and then sits in a database as plain text. HTTPS protects it on the way there. After that, anyone who can run a query can read it, and so can whoever ends up with a leaked backup.

You can avoid that by encrypting the data in the browser before it's sent. Your server stores bytes it can't read, and the key never leaves the user's device.

I built this for CanvasKeep, a diagram app I work on, where drawings are encrypted in the browser before they're saved. I expected to need a crypto library. I didn't. Everything here uses the Web Crypto API that already ships in every modern browser.

We'll build a small page that encrypts a note, keeps the key around between reloads, and lets the user recover that key on another device with a passphrase.

Prerequisites

You'll need to be comfortable with JavaScript, async/await, and Uint8Array (an array of bytes).

Any modern browser works. If you want to run the tests I wrote alongside this, you'll also need Node.js 20 or later, which has the same crypto.subtle API built in.

AES-GCM in two minutes

AES is a symmetric cipher. One key encrypts, and the same key decrypts.

GCM is the mode we'll run it in, and it's the reason I'd pick it as the default. Besides hiding the data, it attaches a 16-byte authentication tag. Change a single bit of the encrypted output and decryption fails loudly. Older modes like AES-CBC don't do that on their own. They'll happily hand you corrupted plaintext.

GCM also needs an IV (initialization vector): 12 random bytes, new ones every time you encrypt. The IV isn't secret. You store it right next to the ciphertext.

The one rule you can't break is this: never reuse an IV with the same key. If two messages share a key and an IV, an attacker can learn things about both of them and forge new ones. Fresh random IVs from crypto.getRandomValues() are fine for a huge number of messages per key, so as long as you generate a new one on every call, you won't have to think about this again.

Generating a key 

export function generateKey(extractable = false) {
  return crypto.subtle.generateKey(
    { name: "AES-GCM", length: 256 },
    extractable,
    ["encrypt", "decrypt"],
  );
}

The first argument picks the algorithm and size. AES comes in 128, 192, and 256 bits, and all three are considered secure. The third argument lists what the key may be used for. A key created with only "encrypt" can't decrypt anything.

The middle argument is the interesting one. With extractable set to false, your code can use the key, but it can never read the key's bytes. crypto.subtle.exportKey just throws.

Why bother? Say your page has an XSS bug, or a bad npm package sneaks some code in. That code can still use the key while the tab is open, and I don't want to pretend otherwise. What it can't do is copy the key and walk off with it. It's a smaller win than it sounds, but I'll take it.

You get back a CryptoKey object, not raw bytes, and you pass that object to everything else.

Encrypting text

The encryption itself is a single call. Most of the code is about getting bytes in and storing the result somewhere you can read it back.

const IV_BYTES = 12;
const FORMAT_VERSION = 1;

// Output layout: [version (1 byte)] [iv (12 bytes)] [ciphertext + 16-byte auth tag]
export async function encryptText(key, text) {
  const iv = crypto.getRandomValues(new Uint8Array(IV_BYTES)); // new IV every time
  const plaintext = new TextEncoder().encode(text);
  const ciphertext = await crypto.subtle.encrypt({ name: "AES-GCM", iv }, key, plaintext);

  const out = new Uint8Array(1 + IV_BYTES + ciphertext.byteLength);
  out[0] = FORMAT_VERSION;
  out.set(iv, 1);
  out.set(new Uint8Array(ciphertext), 1 + IV_BYTES);
  return out;
}

We make a fresh IV (with crypto.getRandomValues, never Math.random()), turn the string into UTF-8 bytes because crypto.subtle only speaks bytes, and encrypt. The result already has the auth tag glued onto the end.

Then we pack it all into one Uint8Array, so it can be stored or uploaded as a single thing:

+---------+----------------+-------------------------------+
| version |       IV       |   ciphertext + auth tag (16)  |
| 1 byte  |    12 bytes    |      same length as text + 16 |
+---------+----------------+-------------------------------+

That first version byte looks like overkill for a demo. I'd still add it. If you ever change the algorithm, the key size, or the layout, your code checks the first byte and knows how to read the old data. CanvasKeep's encrypted diagrams start with one for exactly that reason, and it costs one byte.

One thing that surprised me the first time: encrypt the same text twice and you get two completely different outputs, because the IV changes. That's the point. Someone looking at your database can't even tell that two notes say the same thing.

Decrypting, and what happens when someone changes the data

Decryption unpacks in the same order:

export async function decryptText(key, packed) {
  const bytes = new Uint8Array(packed);
  if (bytes[0] !== FORMAT_VERSION) {
    throw new Error(`Unknown format version: ${bytes[0]}`);
  }
  const iv = bytes.slice(1, 1 + IV_BYTES);
  const ciphertext = bytes.slice(1 + IV_BYTES);
  const plaintext = await crypto.subtle.decrypt({ name: "AES-GCM", iv }, key, ciphertext);
  return new TextDecoder().decode(plaintext);
}

Now flip one bit and see what happens:

const key = await generateKey();
const packed = await encryptText(key, "Hello, encrypted world");

const tampered = packed.slice();
tampered[20] ^= 1; // flip one bit

await decryptText(key, tampered); // throws OperationError

It throws an OperationError. A wrong key throws the same error.

The error tells you nothing about what went wrong, which is annoying while debugging and deliberate on the browser's part. In a real app, catch it and show the user something plain, like "This couldn't be decrypted."

Where to keep the key

A key that vanishes on reload is useless, so it has to live somewhere.

My first instinct was localStorage. But localStorage only stores strings, so you'd have to export the key to put it there, which means making it extractable, which throws away the protection we just set up.

IndexedDB is the better home, because it can store a CryptoKey object as is. The non-extractable flag survives the trip.

const DB_NAME = "my-app-keys";
const STORE = "keys";

function openDB() {
  return new Promise((resolve, reject) => {
    const req = indexedDB.open(DB_NAME, 1);
    req.onupgradeneeded = () => req.result.createObjectStore(STORE);
    req.onsuccess = () => resolve(req.result);
    req.onerror = () => reject(req.error);
  });
}

export async function saveKey(id, key) {
  const db = await openDB();
  return new Promise((resolve, reject) => {
    const tx = db.transaction(STORE, "readwrite");
    tx.objectStore(STORE).put(key, id);
    tx.oncomplete = () => resolve();
    tx.onerror = () => reject(tx.error);
  });
}

export async function loadKey(id) {
  const db = await openDB();
  return new Promise((resolve, reject) => {
    const req = db.transaction(STORE, "readonly").objectStore(STORE).get(id);
    req.onsuccess = () => resolve(req.result ?? null);
    req.onerror = () => reject(req.error);
  });
}

I checked this in Chrome. After a reload, loadKey hands back a CryptoKey with extractable: false, exportKey refuses to touch it, and decryption still works.

There's a catch, and it's a big one. That key exists in one browser on one machine. Clear site data, or open the app on a laptop instead of a desktop, and the key isn't there. Neither is the user's data.

I hit exactly this with CanvasKeep. The key lived in one browser's IndexedDB, so when someone opened their diagrams in a second browser, that browser had no key and couldn't decrypt anything. Fixing it is what the next section is about.

Backing the key up with a passphrase

The idea: encrypt the key itself with a second key that comes from something the user remembers. That encrypted copy can sit on your server, because without the passphrase it's just noise.

Turning a passphrase into a key

You can't use a passphrase as a key directly. It's too short and too guessable. PBKDF2 stretches it by hashing it over and over, so every guess an attacker makes is slow.

const PBKDF2_ITERATIONS = 600_000; // OWASP recommendation for PBKDF2-HMAC-SHA256

async function deriveKeyFromPassphrase(passphrase, salt) {
  const material = await crypto.subtle.importKey(
    "raw",
    new TextEncoder().encode(passphrase),
    "PBKDF2",
    false,
    ["deriveKey"],
  );
  return crypto.subtle.deriveKey(
    { name: "PBKDF2", salt, iterations: PBKDF2_ITERATIONS, hash: "SHA-256" },
    material,
    { name: "AES-GCM", length: 256 },
    false,
    ["wrapKey", "unwrapKey"],
  );
}

The salt is 16 random bytes, different for each user, so nobody can precompute guesses for everyone at once. Like the IV, it isn't secret.

600,000 iterations is what OWASP currently recommends for PBKDF2 with SHA-256. You'll notice the pause. For something a user does once per device, that's fine.

Wrapping the key

"Wrapping" is just encrypting a key with another key. Web Crypto has a method for it:

export async function wrapKeyWithPassphrase(key, passphrase) {
  const salt = crypto.getRandomValues(new Uint8Array(16));
  const iv = crypto.getRandomValues(new Uint8Array(IV_BYTES));
  const wrappingKey = await deriveKeyFromPassphrase(passphrase, salt);
  const wrapped = await crypto.subtle.wrapKey("raw", key, wrappingKey, { name: "AES-GCM", iv });
  return {
    salt: toBase64(salt),
    iv: toBase64(iv),
    wrappedKey: toBase64(new Uint8Array(wrapped)),
    iterations: PBKDF2_ITERATIONS,
  };
}

That object is what you send to your server. Nothing in it is secret on its own.

Getting it back on another device

On the new device, the user types the passphrase and you rebuild the key:

export async function unwrapKeyWithPassphrase(backup, passphrase) {
  const wrappingKey = await deriveKeyFromPassphrase(passphrase, fromBase64(backup.salt));
  return crypto.subtle.unwrapKey(
    "raw",
    fromBase64(backup.wrappedKey),
    wrappingKey,
    { name: "AES-GCM", iv: fromBase64(backup.iv) },
    { name: "AES-GCM", length: 256 },
    false,
    ["encrypt", "decrypt"],
  );
}

See the false near the bottom? The key comes back non-extractable, ready to drop into IndexedDB. A wrong passphrase makes unwrapKey throw, since the wrapped key is protected by GCM too.

The part that tripped me up

wrapKey needs to read the key's bytes to encrypt them, so it only works on an extractable key. That seems to clash with everything I said earlier about keeping keys non-extractable.

It works out if you do things in order. Create the key as extractable, make the backup straight away, then store a non-extractable copy and drop the original:

export async function lockKey(key) {
  const raw = await crypto.subtle.exportKey("raw", key);
  return crypto.subtle.importKey("raw", raw, { name: "AES-GCM" }, false, ["encrypt", "decrypt"]);
}

Once that's done, nothing on the page can export the key again.

The snippets above lean on two small helpers for converting bytes to base64 and back:

export function toBase64(bytes) {
  let binary = "";
  for (const b of bytes) binary += String.fromCharCode(b);
  return btoa(binary);
}

export function fromBase64(base64) {
  const binary = atob(base64);
  const bytes = new Uint8Array(binary.length);
  for (let i = 0; i < binary.length; i++) bytes[i] = binary.charCodeAt(i);
  return bytes;
}

The finished page

Here's everything wired together. To keep it self-contained, localStorage stands in for the server. In a real app that line would be a fetch() to your API, and only the ciphertext would go over the wire.

<textarea id="note">Meeting notes: launch on Friday.</textarea>
<button id="save">Encrypt and save</button>
<button id="load">Load and decrypt</button>

<h2>What the server would store</h2>
<pre id="stored">(nothing yet)</pre>

<h2>Decrypted</h2>
<pre id="output">(nothing yet)</pre>

<script type="module">
  import { generateKey, encryptText, decryptText, toBase64, fromBase64 } from "./crypto.js";
  import { saveKey, loadKey } from "./key-store.js";

  const $ = (id) => document.getElementById(id);

  async function getKey() {
    let key = await loadKey("notes");
    if (!key) {
      key = await generateKey(false); // non-extractable
      await saveKey("notes", key);
    }
    return key;
  }

  $("stored").textContent = localStorage.getItem("note") ?? "(nothing yet)";

  $("save").onclick = async () => {
    const key = await getKey();
    const packed = await encryptText(key, $("note").value);
    // Stand-in for a fetch() to your API: only ciphertext goes over the wire.
    localStorage.setItem("note", toBase64(packed));
    $("stored").textContent = localStorage.getItem("note");
  };

  $("load").onclick = async () => {
    const stored = localStorage.getItem("note");
    if (!stored) return;
    const key = await getKey();
    try {
      $("output").textContent = await decryptText(key, fromBase64(stored));
    } catch {
      $("output").textContent = "Could not decrypt: wrong key or the data was changed.";
    }
  };
</script>

Serve the folder with any static server (npx serve is fine). ES modules won't load from a file:// URL. Type a note and hit "Encrypt and save", and the middle box fills with base64 that means nothing without the key. Reload, hit "Load and decrypt", and your note is back.

Mistakes I'd watch out for

Reusing an IV is the big one. Call crypto.getRandomValues for a new IV on every single encrypt, no exceptions.

Exporting keys into localStorage is the next. It works, and it quietly undoes the point of non-extractable keys. Store the CryptoKey in IndexedDB instead.

Don't invent your own crypto, either. No clever XOR tricks, no Math.random() for keys or IVs. crypto.subtle and crypto.getRandomValues are all you need.

Plan for lost keys from day one. If the key is gone, the data is gone, and users will not find that as interesting as you do.

And be honest about what this protects. It keeps data safe on your server and in your backups. It does nothing for a page that's already running malicious code while the user is on it.

Where to go from here

The next step I'd take is one key per document. Give each document its own key and wrap that key with the user's main key. Then you can share one document without exposing the rest. That's how CanvasKeep handles diagrams.

Passphrases get forgotten, so a recovery key is worth adding too: wrap the same key a second time with a long random code the user writes down somewhere.

Once each document has its own key, you can share it with a link that carries the key in the URL. That's the next article.

Wrapping up

None of this needs a library. AES-GCM encrypts and catches tampering, non-extractable keys can't be read out by scripts, IndexedDB keeps them across reloads, and PBKDF2 plus wrapKey gets users back in on a new device. The full code, tests included, is about 150 lines.

I use this approach in CanvasKeep, a diagram app where drawings are encrypted in your browser before they're saved.
